Deux communautés, un même deuil : retour: Two communities, one grief: a look back at the tributes to Mohamed Benredouane and Michael Mizrahi after the shooting.
Mohamed Lamine Benredouane et Michel Miz: Mohamed Lamine Benredouane and Michel Mizrahi.
C’est un sujet difficile. La tragédie su: This is a difficult subject. The tragedy in Côte-des-Neiges has deeply affected the victims’ families, their loved ones and their communities, but also Quebec society as a whole. Like many people, I came across videos of the shooting that were very hard to watch – in which Mohamed Lamine Benredouane, Michel Mizrahi and the gunman are seen being killed.
Dans les heures qui ont suivi le drame,: In the hours after the tragedy, I also read various reactions on social media. One of them, shared by Abdellah Azzouz, pointed out that in this story, “Mohamed” was the hero. That sentence stayed with me. It challenged certain reflexes, certain prejudices, and the way a first name, an origin or an affiliation can quickly shape how we read an event.
À partir de là, j’ai voulu comprendre. P: From there, I wanted to understand. Not just to report the facts, but to tell this tragedy in a human way, by going to meet those who knew Mohamed Lamine Benredouane and Michel Mizrahi. I wanted to cover their funerals with as much respect as possible, keeping at the centre the people they were: men, loved ones, fathers, friends, important members of their communities.
Cet article n’a pas été écrit pour rédui: This article was not written to reduce their story to an affiliation, a religion, an origin or a uniform. On the contrary, it seeks to remind us that before the debates, the reactions and the comments, there were human lives, brutally cut short.
Merci à toutes les personnes qui ont acc: Thank you to everyone who agreed to speak with me at such a painful time. My most sincere condolences to the victims’ families and loved ones.
<strong>Le 22 juin 2026, peu avant midi,: On June 22, 2026, shortly before noon, an armed attack in the Côte-des-Neiges neighbourhood left three people dead: Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) officer Mohamed Lamine Benredouane; civilian Michel Moshe Mizrahi – whose exact circumstances of death are still under investigation by the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), Quebec’s independent investigations bureau – and the gunman, Seth Scott Hatfield.
<strong>Dans les heures qui ont suivi, l: In the hours that followed, images of the shooting spread rapidly on social media. They were shared, commented on and analyzed before all the information had even been confirmed. According to loved ones, some family members learned of the death of one of their own through the media or through images circulated online.
<strong>Très vite, la tragédie a quitté: Very quickly, the tragedy left the scene of the attack and replayed itself on social media, where many tried to interpret it based on the origin, religion, first name, uniform or presumed affiliation of the people involved.
<strong>Sur le terrain, pourtant, les ho: On the ground, however, the tributes tell a more complex story: a Muslim police officer named Mohamed mourned across Greater Montréal, despite deep distrust of the police, and a Jewish man, Michel Moshe Mizrahi, who, as of today, there is nothing to suggest was targeted because of his religion, and whom his loved ones describe as a man who tried to help others get to safety. In these two mourning processes, La Converse examines the reflexes, fears and prejudices that such a tragedy can reveal.
<strong>Au Petit Maghreb, une minute de: In Little Maghreb, a minute of silence before the match
Le soir du 22 juin, quelques heures aprè: On the evening of June 22, a few hours after the attack in Côte-des-Neiges, Algeria was playing Jordan at the World Cup. On Jean-Talon, in the heart of Little Maghreb, Algerian fans had gathered as they often do on match nights. But this time, the mood was somber.
Avant le début du match, les supporteurs: Before the match began, the Algerian fans observed a minute of silence to honour Mohamed Lamine Benredouane, an SPVM officer of Algerian origin who had been killed earlier that day. In the crowd, the flags, jerseys and chants gave way, for a moment, to a heavy silence.
Ce moment dit déjà quelque chose de la c: This moment already says something about the complexity of this tragedy. Mohamed Lamine Benredouane was a police officer, but he was also Mohamed. He wore the SPVM uniform, but he also carried a first name, an origin and a history in which many people saw themselves. In a context where some comments posted on social media were already linking the attack to Islam or immigration, this minute of silence was a reminder of a reality that is harder to squeeze into categories: this time, the “Mohamed” in the story is the one who fell protecting citizens.
Le lendemain soir, La Converse se rend d: The next evening, La Converse returned to Little Maghreb. Several people agreed to speak, but anonymously and without showing their faces. The fear was palpable. Some said they feared being recognized, while others raised the possibility of reprisals, fines or tensions with police officers in the area.
Les récentes révélations au sujet de com: The recent revelations about racist behaviour at neighbourhood police station 39 (PDQ 39) in Montréal-Nord quickly came up in conversations. “With what happened at PDQ 39, we see how they treat us, and it scares us,” said one person we met there. For many, trust in the police remains fragile, sometimes even broken.
Mais la mort de Mohamed Lamine Benredoua: But the death of Mohamed Lamine Benredouane complicates this relationship. Those who speak of distrust toward the police as an institution also speak of sorrow, respect and solidarity with the fallen man. In the remarks gathered on Jean-Talon, one idea kept coming back: beyond the uniform, it is also “one of ours” who died. A brother, a son, a man from a community that, despite its wounds and fears, wanted to pay tribute to him.

<strong>Sur la route du dernier hommage<: On the road to the final tribute
Laval, Wednesday, June 24, 2026, 8 p.m. On Quebec’s Fête nationale, the mood is usually one of celebration. This year, for many citizens, colleagues and families, Saint-Jean looks completely different.
Bien avant d’arriver au Cimetière islami: Well before reaching the Hamza Islamic Cemetery, the first tributes to Mohamed Lamine Benredouane appear. Along Highway 15 toward Laval, under a cloudy sky, Laval police officers and firefighters are stationed on several overpasses above the road. Quebec and SPVM flags hang from the guardrails. As their colleague’s funeral procession passes, they all pay a final salute, hand against forehead.
À mesure que l’on approche du cimetière,: As you get closer to the cemetery, traffic gets denser. The parking lots quickly fill up. Police officers direct drivers to makeshift spots, including along the bike path on Boulevard Lévesque Est. From there, it’s still about a fifteen-minute walk to the cemetery.
Sur le trajet, une foule de citoyens ava: Along the way, a crowd of citizens moves in the same direction. Men, women, children, elders; people of different origins, religious affiliations and communities converge on the same place. In the crowd, a young man makes his way with difficulty on crutches. Everyone seems driven by the same desire: to pay a final tribute to Mohamed Lamine Benredouane.
Le trajet traverse un quartier résidenti: The route passes through a residential neighbourhood. In front of several houses, families have come out onto their front steps to watch the silent procession of hundreds of people heading toward the cemetery. The closer we get, the more silence takes hold.
À l’intérieur du cimetière, les rangées: Inside the cemetery, the rows of people who have come to pay a final tribute to Mohamed Lamine stretch a long way, well beyond where he lies. The faces around the grave are marked by emotion, eyes often lowered.
Âgé de 34 ans et originaire de Skikda, e: Mohamed Lamine Benredouane, 34, originally from Skikda, Algeria, leaves behind his wife, who is pregnant with their second child, and a three-year-old child.
Les collègues du policier, presque tous: The officer’s colleagues, almost all dressed in black, hold his portrait in their hands, along with white flowers. Only a few officers are still in uniform. Embraces follow one after another. Some exchange a few words in low voices, others wipe away tears while loved ones receive the many people who have come to offer their condolences.
Lorsque l’imam prend la parole, le silen: When the imam speaks, silence settles. All eyes remain on him. At each invocation (du’a), hundreds of voices rise in unison: “Amin.” A moment of reflection accompanies the prayers for Mohamed Lamine Benredouane.
Dans son allocution, l’imam rappelle que: In his address, the imam reminds those present that in Islam, it is important to remember a person’s good deeds and pass them on after their death, since they continue to benefit them. He describes the deceased as a devoted man.
« Mohamed Lamine était un homme serviabl: “Mohamed Lamine was a helpful man, always ready to help others. Every morning, he left his home to do his duty and protect citizens, leaving behind his wife and his child, never knowing whether he would come home safe and sound.”
L’imam le qualifie ensuite de <em>shahīd: The imam then calls him a shahīd (شهيد), a term that refers, in Islamic tradition, to a person considered to have died as a martyr. According to him, Mohamed Lamine earned this status because he lost his life protecting citizens in the line of duty. He stresses that, in the Muslim tradition, dying as a shahīd is considered one of the most honourable deaths.
<strong>« Momo était la définition même: “Momo was the very definition of a positive leader”
Pour plusieurs de ses collègues, Mohamed: For many of his colleagues, Mohamed Lamine Benredouane leaves the memory of a deeply committed police officer, but above all of a man liked by everyone.
« Momo était la définition même d’un lea: “Momo was the very definition of a positive leader,” says one of them, pausing as if the words failed him. “You couldn’t spend two seconds with him without laughing. He brought people together and led by example.”
Selon ce policier, qui préfère garder l’: According to this officer, who prefers to remain anonymous, Mohamed paid great attention to detail. Before every shift, he arrived early to carefully prepare his equipment, a habit he had kept since his training at the École nationale de police du Québec a few years earlier. He polished his boots, cleaned his gear and made sure his uniform was impeccable. “He wanted the police to look good,” he explains.
Ayant grandi à Côte-des-Neiges jusqu’à l: Having grown up in Côte-des-Neiges until his teens, Mohamed had chosen to come back and work there as a police officer. According to his colleagues, he had excellent relationships with residents and was liked as much by the community as by his fellow officers. “He loved what he did. His mission was always to help others, no matter when,” one of them sums up.
Au poste de quartier 26, où travaillent: At neighbourhood station 26, where about 170 officers work, his name was known to everyone, his colleague says. “Everybody knew him, everybody talked to him.”
Plusieurs policiers rencontrés affirment: Several officers we spoke with say his death has deeply shaken not only the members of PDQ 26, but the entire SPVM. One of them confides that since Monday’s events, there have been few reasons to smile. According to him, it was only after the ceremony, seeing colleagues, loved ones and family members gathered around Mohamed, that some found, for a moment, a bit of comfort.
Les pas se succèdent lentement vers les: Footsteps slowly make their way toward the parking lots while the family continues to receive condolences. At the cemetery exit, conversations gradually resume. Several people recall memories of Mohamed, while others say they hope his death will lead people to question certain prejudices that are still very much present.
Un agent de police, qui préfère conserve: A police officer, who prefers to remain anonymous, takes a few moments to share his thoughts.
« Quand les gens entendent le prénom “Mo: “When people hear the name ‘Mohamed,’ some have preconceived ideas. This time, the Mohamed in question wasn’t the terrorist. He was the police officer who lost his life protecting citizens. I hope it makes some people think.”
Quelques jours plus tard, Amine Tessa, c: A few days later, Amine Tessa, an activist content creator on social media, echoes this view. According to him, the first hours after the shooting were marked by rumours that quickly fed certain stereotypes.
« Dès qu’il est question d’une attaque c: “As soon as there’s an attack like that, some people immediately link the crime to an immigrant. You see comments like ‘It’s another Muslim’ or ‘Import the Third World, become the Third World,’” he tells us.
Pour Amine, le fait que ce soit finaleme: For Amine, the fact that it was ultimately a police officer named Mohamed who lost his life protecting citizens should lead us to question these reflexes.
Lorsque l’identité des victimes et du ti: When the identities of the victims and the gunman were finally confirmed, the picture was entirely different: Mohamed Lamine Benredouane, the officer who died during the police intervention, is a Quebecer of Algerian origin; Michel Mizrahi, the civilian who died, is a Quebecer born in Lebanon and a well-known member of the Jewish community of Côte Saint-Luc; and the gunman is a Canadian from Alberta.
Cette tendance à interpréter rapidement: This tendency to quickly interpret the tragedy through the lens of affiliation also appears in the reflection of Mohamed Lotfi, a journalist and artist, published the day after the shooting. In his text, he states that he does not seek to analyze the gunman’s motives, “but rather to question our collective way of reacting to death and suffering out of an instinct of fear.”
Pour lui, « cette séquence médiatique a: For him, “this media sequence revealed a phenomenon that has become familiar”: “No sooner were the victims identified than the conversation began to organize itself around affiliations.” According to Mr. Lotfi, the first reactions, particularly on social media, showed how quickly, in a moment of crisis, people can be turned into symbols, sometimes even before the facts are fully established.
« Lorsqu’une société se laisse gouverner: “When a society lets itself be governed by fear, it simplifies everything. It turns human beings into symbols. It replaces faces with affiliations,” he writes.
Cette logique, que Mohamed Lotfi décrit: This logic, which Mohamed Lotfi describes as “one of the deepest illnesses of our time,” pushes people to comment, to interpret and to pick a side before even taking the time to see the people behind the identities attributed to them.
Amine Tessa insiste sur la nécessité de: Amine Tessa insists on the need for caution. He understands why Mohamed’s origins are being mentioned now to dismantle certain prejudices. He warns, however, against the risk of reducing a person to their origin. “I don’t want us to fall into that game. At the end of the day, a Quebecer is a Quebecer. A first name, an origin or a religion says nothing about a person’s courage and values,” he concludes.
Les proches de Mohamed, eux, préfèrent p: Mohamed’s loved ones, for their part, prefer to talk about the person they knew. All paint a portrait of a man deeply devoted to his family, always smiling, positive and generous. His voice breaking, still shaken by the events, one of them says: “Mohamed didn’t deserve to die, much less to be killed by that individual.”
Sur le terrain, dans Côte-des-Neiges, pl: On the ground in Côte-des-Neiges, several young people say they are “deeply touched” by the death of Officer Benredouane. They explain that they had crossed paths with him several times in the course of his work as a police officer. “It’s true that as young people, we have preconceptions about the police, but he always treated us with respect,” says one of them. All the young people we spoke with describe him as “a really good person.”
Les hommages au défunt ne s’arrêtent tou: The tributes to the deceased do not end with this ceremony, however. The SPVM has announced that he will be given a civic funeral open to the public on July 7 at the Bell Centre.
Le même jour, à quelques kilomètres du c: That same day, a few kilometres from the Hamza Islamic Cemetery, another family and another community gathered to mourn and say goodbye to Michel Mizrahi, the civilian killed by a female police officer in the same tragedy.

Dans les premières heures qui suivent la: In the first hours after the shooting, when little information had yet been confirmed, rumours pointed to a possible antisemitic attack. Here again, the tragedy was quickly read through the lens of affiliation. The accounts gathered afterward, however, complicate this initial version of the story: according to the information available to date, Michel Mizrahi was not targeted because of his Jewish identity. Several members of the community say instead that during the first exchange of gunfire, he tried to help people get to safety.
Le lendemain de la fusillade, le conseil: The day after the shooting, Côte Saint-Luc city councillor Mike Cohen posted a video on Instagram in which he goes to the Beth Chabad synagogue, where the community was already beginning to gather to pay tribute to Michel Mizrahi.
« Toute la communauté est sous le choc »: “The whole community is in shock,” he says.
Âgé de 68 ans, Michel Mizrahi résidait à: Michel Mizrahi, 68, lived in Côte Saint-Luc and had attended this synagogue for many years. According to Mike Cohen, he worked in the custom clothing business and was in the Côte-des-Neiges area for work at the time of the attack. He was then supposed to meet his son for coffee at Heal, a meeting that would never happen…
Mike Cohen ajoute que, selon des membres: Mike Cohen adds that, according to members of the synagogue, Michel had health problems, but faced them with great courage and stoicism.
Le rabbin, qui côtoyait Michel Mizrahi d: The rabbi, who had known Michel Mizrahi for many years at Beth Chabad, remembers “a man of great kindness,” always smiling and always ready to help others. He recalls that Michel came regularly to the synagogue with his son and had a seat in his name, labelled “Mizrahi Michel – C8.”
Selon le rabbin, plusieurs témoignages r: According to the rabbi, several accounts gathered after the tragedy indicate that Michel Mizrahi helped a mother and her child get to safety before losing his life. “He sacrificed himself for others,” he sums up.
Le mercredi 24 juin, à 9 h 45, sous un c: On Wednesday, June 24, at 9:45 a.m., under a clear sky, family, friends and members of the Jewish community gather at the Paperman & Sons funeral home to say goodbye to Michel Mizrahi.
À l’intérieur, la foule est si dense que: Inside, the crowd is so dense that many people remain standing all the way into the entrance. When the coffin is carried outside, embraces multiply. Loved ones hold each other for a long time. Many of those present wear sunglasses behind which, at times, tears can be glimpsed.
Dans le stationnement du salon funéraire: In the funeral home parking lot, community members say that in the moments after the shooting began, Michel Mizrahi instinctively pushed people into a neighbouring business to get them to safety, saving their lives.
Parmi les personnes venues lui rendre un: Among those who came to pay their final respects is Alain Pereque, a friend of Michel’s since their childhood in Beirut, Lebanon. He describes him as “a man with a big heart, always positive, always smiling.”
« C’est ça, Michel », dit-il simplement,: “That’s Michel,” he says simply, his voice heavy with emotion.
Sur les réseaux sociaux, les témoignages: On social media, tributes keep pouring in: “He was an extraordinary man,” “What an incredible man, gone too soon,” “A beautiful soul has left this world too soon. We miss you, Michel.” Hundreds of messages that all say the same thing: Michel Mizrahi mattered and leaves an immense void in his community.
Dans le cas de Michel Mizrahi, comme de: In the case of Michel Mizrahi, as with Mohamed Lamine Benredouane, the first accounts quickly put affiliation front and centre. Yet these two men, whom everything seemed to separate, were brought together by the same tragedy, caused by the violence of a white man.
Le 24 juin 2026, leurs proches leur ont: On June 24, 2026, their loved ones paid tribute to them, not as symbols, but as beloved people. Two lives brutally cut short, two communities in mourning, and one lesson left silently to all.
Fusillade de Côte-des-Neiges : les homma: Côte-des-Neiges Shooting: Tributes to Mohamed Benredouane and Michel Mizrahi Beyond Prejudice
La fusillade de Côte-des-Neiges, survenu: The Côte-des-Neiges shooting on June 22, 2026, claimed the lives of SPVM officer Mohamed Lamine Benredouane, civilian Michel Mizrahi and the gunman, Seth Scott Hatfield. Through the tributes paid to the two victims, this La Converse report explores the rumours, prejudices and identity-based reflexes that marked the first hours of the tragedy, while highlighting the lives of two men whom their communities remember above all for their courage, generosity and humanity.
